title: Why Wrestler Jordan Burroughs Hasn't Transitioned Into MMA
guestName: Why Wrestler Jordan Burroughs Hasn't Transitioned Into MMA
guestBio: This clip is taken from the Joe Rogan Experience #1591 with Jordan Burroughs. https://open.spotify.com/episode/6j9JygkIR2MsNLGZA9Suc3?si=NxQjcsEhRYes8yDW9gHYmg
tldr: Jordan Burroughs explains why his love for pure wrestling has kept him from pursuing an MMA career despite his elite grappling credentials
Discussion of the financial and platform tradeoffs between staying in wrestling versus chasing UFC money and exposure
Breakdown of what an MMA transition would actually require — years of striking and submission defense development he's not willing to invest
Burroughs reflects on the mental difference between wrestling's structure and the unpredictable demands of competing in mixed martial arts
Joe pushes on whether any scenario exists where Burroughs makes the jump, and the answer is an honest but firm probably not
Broader conversation about why elite wrestling backgrounds produce so many MMA champions even when the wrestlers themselves don't cross over
recap:
Jordan Burroughs is one of the most decorated wrestlers in American history. A two-time Olympic medalist, multiple-time world champion, and widely regarded as one of the most technically gifted freestyle wrestlers of his generation, Burroughs sits down with Joe Rogan for an honest conversation about the question that every combat sports fan has asked about him: why hasn't he tried MMA?

The answer, Burroughs explains, is more deliberate than people realize. It isn't fear of the unknown, and it isn't that he doubts his ability to compete. It comes down to something more personal: he genuinely loves wrestling. Unlike many elite grapplers who view their sport as a stepping stone to the UFC's bigger platform and bigger paychecks, Burroughs has built his entire identity around being the best pure wrestler on earth. Making the move to MMA would mean giving up the thing he actually cares about most.

Joe pushes him on the financial argument. UFC fighters at the top of the card make serious money, and the exposure is incomparable. Burroughs acknowledges that, but he points out that wrestling success has opened up its own opportunities in coaching, sponsorships, and legacy-building. He isn't walking away from money by staying in wrestling. He's choosing a different kind of career.

They dig into the mechanics of the MMA transition. Burroughs talks about what it would actually require to be competitive. A wrestler of his caliber would have elite-level takedowns and ground control from day one, but the boxing, Muay Thai, and especially the submission defense would take years to develop properly. He doesn't believe in making that jump halfway. If he were going to do it, he would want to do it right, and doing it right would require stepping away from competitive wrestling for multiple years.

The conversation also touches on the mental side of it. Wrestling has a structure, a community, and a scoring system that Burroughs understands completely. MMA is a different world with different rhythms. He talks about watching MMA from the outside and appreciating it as a fan without feeling the pull to compete in it that some wrestlers feel.

Joe asks directly whether there's any scenario where he makes the move. Burroughs is honest: never say never, but the window is closing, and his heart has always been in the singlet rather than the shorts. He'd rather be remembered as the greatest freestyle wrestler of his generation than as a middling MMA prospect who tried to cash in on a famous wrestling pedigree.

The clip ends with a broader discussion of what wrestling does for an athlete's combat IQ and why so many of the best MMA fighters have elite wrestling backgrounds, even if Burroughs himself chooses to stay in the sport where he's already proven himself at the absolute highest level.
